## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so I can't separate the network from the recipe. The default budget gives only about 131k steps, which is 32 updates of 4,096 samples. That looks too few updates to learn exact multi-brick builds, and a reward per brick of about 0.05 to 0.2 is close in size to the entropy bonus, which may hold the policy back. My first guess is that the recipe is the main bottleneck. Fewer PPO epochs buy more samples, and smaller batches give many more updates. A lower entropy coefficient and a slightly longer horizon should make the +1 bonus for an exact build count for more. I test two recipes on the unchanged network: 2 epochs (P1) and 1 epoch with a higher learning rate (P3). P2 keeps P1's recipe but adds a footprint-shaped head, so P1 vs P2 isolates the network change and P1 vs P3 isolates the recipe change.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored 0 on dev, and training success in the last 10% of training was also 0. That held for 178k to 408k steps, with 1 or 2 PPO epochs and with either the pooled or the footprint-conv head. More data and more updates did not help, so the recipe alone is probably not the bottleneck. The baseline can in principle express a good 1x1 or 2x2 placement rule: a cell is fillable when its height is z and the target cell at layer z is missing. Even so, it never succeeds, not even on small designs during training. Two explanations remain. (1) The world differs from the description in how actions map to cells: the anchor, the axis order or the type order may differ. All our heads assume a per-cell match between features and actions, so they could never learn. (2) The layer-selection logic is too hard to learn at this budget. This round tests both, using r1c3's maximum-data recipe so that only the architecture changes.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0, with 0 training success, on every seed. The heads were aligned, dense and per-layer, and the recipes ranged from 1 to 4 epochs and 131k to 408k steps. So head alignment and data volume are not the main blocker. My leading guess, which these results do not test directly, is that early learning collapses onto DONE. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0. DONE is a single cheap logit seen in every softmax, so PPO can learn it quickly. Low entropy (0.003) then shuts off exploration before the placement head learns which cells are safe. The three candidates share one anti-collapse recipe: entropy 0.02 and the DONE output starting at zero and scaled by 0.2 so it learns slowly. On top of that they test the baseline net, the per-layer head, and a deeper column MLP with a separate critic. Any score above 0 would be informative.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also 0 on train success. That held across recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs, entropy from 0.003 to 0.02), heads (pooled, footprint-conv, per-layer and dense) and the slow-DONE fix. Small differences are not what is going on: something stops any success at all. The task says the world may not behave as described, so the likeliest blocker is a mismatch between action indices and cells. Every aligned head assumes a top-left anchor and the stated y/x order. The dense head could have learned any mapping, but it probably learns too slowly on about 400k samples. A cheap hedge is a learned local window for each brick type: a 3x3 conv covers top-left, centred and bottom-right anchors, and adding transposed features covers a y/x swap. The legality mask also reveals the anchor convention and orientation, so feeding it in as an input should help. These are last-round bets aimed at getting any nonzero score.
